1. Scientific Analysis

Analysis Type

Scale-matched LoG band-pass blob detection (dark polarity) sized to ~80 nm particles, threshold_rel tuned by overlay inspection, de-duplicated within one radius, conditional distance-transform watershed (peak_local_max markers, min_distance ~ radius) to split touching cores, then per-particle sizing.

Interpretation

The analysis detects Au nanospheres in a TEM field via scale-matched LoG blob detection (dark polarity) at pixel_size 0.3955 nm/px (from the 810 nm field-of-view over 2048 px). The dense mask fraction (~0.26) and packing of the raw image indicate a near-monolayer of spheres. Physically, the dark blobs are the electron-dense Au cores (mass-thickness contrast in TEM); their circular projections and near-uniform darkness are consistent with solid metallic spheres rather than aggregates or hollow shells. The measured size distribution is strongly unimodal (a single dominant histogram bin at ~69–72 nm containing 51 of 120 particles, median 69.6 nm, mean 70.1 nm, SD 8.1 nm ~12% CV), which is the signature of a monodisperse colloidal synthesis. The tail of small readings (a handful at 45–58 nm) and a few large (85–98 nm) most plausibly reflect edge-clipped particles at the field boundary and occasional off-center LoG placement in the tightly packed field rather than a true second population — supported by watershed not being triggered (no merged components; single-particle area ~32k px matches one sphere), so the distribution is not fragmented by over-segmentation. Importantly, the analysis undercounts: at the conservative thr_rel=0.4 chosen to suppress speckle, only ~120 of the visibly present spheres are marked, with clear gaps in the overlay (lower-left/central regions). The measured median sits ~13% below the 80 nm nominal — this gap is partly real (LoG/threshold sizing measures a band-pass core response, which tends to under-report the geometric diameter for touching, high-contrast dark disks) and means the absolute diameter is a lower bound, while the relative spread (monodispersity) is robust.

2. Visualizations

Original Image
Analysis Visualization

3. Scientific Claims

Claim 1: The Au nanosphere population is monodisperse with a unimodal diameter distribution centered at a median of 69.6 nm (mean 70.1 nm, SD 8.1 nm, ~12% CV) across 120 detected particles; the true diameter is likely a lower bound relative to the 80 nm nominal owing to band-pass/threshold sizing bias.

Scientific Impact: A single narrow size mode confirms a well-controlled, monodisperse colloidal synthesis suitable for applications requiring uniform optical/plasmonic response; quantifying the sizing bias (~13% below nominal) flags that LoG-core diameters should be calibrated against edge-based measurements before reporting absolute size.

Literature Search Query: Has anyone quantified the systematic under-sizing of LoG band-pass core detection relative to edge-based diameter measurement for densely packed, high-contrast nanospheres in TEM?

Keywords: gold nanoparticles, monodispersity, TEM particle sizing, size distribution, LoG blob detection

4. Caveats & Limitations

Detection is incomplete: the conservative threshold (thr_rel=0.4, chosen to suppress speckle) leaves visibly present spheres unmarked (overlay gaps in lower-left/central regions), so N=120 underestimates the true population by an unquantified margin — the count should be treated as a lower bound, not a density measurement. Absolute diameters are biased low (median ~13% under the 80 nm nominal) because band-pass/threshold sizing measures the core response rather than the geometric edge; small-tail readings (45–58 nm) are plausibly edge-clipped boundary particles rather than a genuine second population. Only 91 of 120 are interior particles, so boundary truncation affects ~24% of measurements. No shape/solidity metrics were extracted to independently confirm sphericity vs. faceting.
